summary: Describes a way to automatically, authenticatedly update DNSSEC trust anchors, protecting against compromise of N-1 of N keys. It needs resolver management changes and one new flag bit in the DNSKEY record. It is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: A safe way for a computer to swap the first key it trusts for a new one without anyone doing it by hand.

questions: how do resolvers update trust anchors
how do dnssec trust anchors update automatically
what is the dnskey revoke bit
subtitle: How a DNSSEC validating resolver can safely accept new trust anchors, and drop old ones, without a human editing its configuration.

tldr.problem: A DNSSEC resolver needs a trust anchor for each signed island it validates, and manually replacing those keys on every resolver when a key is rolled or compromised is hard to do.
tldr.mechanism: A new key is accepted if the existing trust anchors sign the DNSKEY RRSet that carries it and it stays there for a hold-down time. A REVOKE flag bit in the DNSKEY record lets a key retire itself immediately and permanently.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers can follow key rollovers on their own, and the scheme can recover from N-1 compromised keys out of N. It does not solve initial trust anchor configuration, and if every key at a trust point is compromised, a manual update is still needed.

facts.label: REVOKE flag
facts.value: Bit 8 of the DNSKEY Flags field

facts.label: Add hold-down
facts.value: 30 days (or original TTL expiry, if greater)

facts.label: Minimum SEP keys per trust point

today: RFC 5011 is an Internet Standard, and the unit's metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of automated DNSSEC trust anchor updates.

sections.title: The Trust Anchor Problem
sections.content:
DNSSEC will not be one single signed name space. It will be islands of signed names, each starting at a trust point in the DNS tree. The association of a trust point name with one of its public keys is called a trust anchor, and a trust point can have more than one.

A validating resolver must know a trust anchor for any branch it wants to validate. Because signed islands may be separated by unsigned parts of the tree, a resolver may need to know literally thousands of them. Managing these by hand is problematic, and it gets worse when a trust anchor key has to be replaced.

This RFC describes how a resolver can update the trust anchors for a trust point mostly without human intervention. It does not cover how trust anchors are first configured in a resolver.
sections.eli5: A computer needs to remember the right key for each part of the internet it checks. If those keys had to be swapped by a person every time, it would be a never-ending chore.

sections.title: Revocation and Add Hold-Down
sections.content:
The core idea: existing trust anchors can vouch for new ones at the same place in the hierarchy. When a zone operator adds a new SEP key (a DNSKEY with the Secure Entry Point bit set) to the trust point DNSKEY RRSet, and an existing trust anchor validates that RRSet, the resolver can add the new key to its trust anchors. Two problems must be handled.

Revocation. Suppose keys A and B are trust anchors and B is compromised. Without a revoke mechanism, B could publish a signed key set that leaves out A. So revoking a key requires knowing its private key: a key is revoked when the resolver sees it, with the REVOKE bit set, in a self-signed RRSet. Revocation is immediate and permanent, and the revoked key may only be used to validate the signature over that revoking DNSKEY RRSet. In the example, the attacker can revoke B but not A.

Add hold-down. An attacker holding B could add a new key C and then revoke the good keys. To mitigate this, the resolver starts an acceptance timer when it sees a new SEP key in a validated DNSKEY RRSet and remembers which keys validated it. If a validly signed RRSet appears without the new key, or all of the keys that validated it are revoked before the timer ends, the timer is reset. The resolver MUST NOT treat the new key as a trust anchor until the hold-down time expires and it has then fetched and validated a DNSKEY RRSet containing the key. The owner can recover by revoking B and adding a new key D, signing with both A and B.

The hold-down only mitigates the attack. An attacker with one compromised key could keep a single resolver unaware by intercepting the real data and substituting its own, signed only by that key. The RFC calls this no worse than the current situation with a compromised key.
sections.eli5: A trusted friend can introduce a new friend, but you wait a month before believing it, in case a trickster is pretending. And if a friend loses their secret handshake, they can announce it, and you stop trusting that handshake forever.

sections.title: Refresh Timing, Hold-Down Times and the REVOKE Bit
sections.content:
A resolver set up for automatic updates MUST query the trust point's DNSKEY RRSet and related RRSIG records on a schedule: queryInterval = MAX(1 hr, MIN(15 days, 1/2*OrigTTL, 1/2*RRSigExpirationInterval)). If a query fails, it retries with retryTime = MAX(1 hour, MIN(1 day, .1*origTTL, .1*expireInterval)).

  • Add hold-down time: 30 days or the expiration of the original TTL of the first DNSKEY RRSet that contained the new key, whichever is greater. This ensures at least two validated RRSets containing the new key are seen before acceptance.
  • Remove hold-down time: 30 days. This is only bookkeeping for the key database; failing to purge defunct keys does not hurt security.
  • Minimum trust anchors per trust point: a compliant resolver MUST be able to manage at least five SEP keys per trust point.

The only change to the wire format is one flag: bit 8 of the DNSKEY Flags field is the REVOKE flag. Set to 1, and seen with an RRSIG over the DNSKEY RRSet made by that same key, it makes the key permanently invalid for everything except validating the revocation. Because the bit changes the record, a DNSKEY with REVOKE set has a different fingerprint than one without it, which affects matching against DS records in the parent.
sections.eli5: The computer checks in on a schedule, like checking the mailbox, and waits 30 days before trusting a new key. Marking a key as retired is just flipping one tiny switch on it.

sections.title: The Key State Table
sections.content:
The normative heart of the RFC is a state table describing how a resolver views each key at a trust point. A key starts in Start.

  • Start: the key does not yet exist as a trust anchor at the resolver.
  • AddPend: the key has been seen in a validated DNSKEY RRSet with its SEP bit set, and its hold-down is running.
  • Valid: the key has been in every validated DNSKEY RRSet through the hold-down, so it can verify RRSets. The RRSet need not be continuously present (its TTL may expire), but whenever it is seen and validated, the key must be in it, otherwise a KeyRem event occurs.
  • Missing: an abnormal state. The key stays a valid trust point key but was absent from the last validated RRSet, because the operator should use the REVOKE bit before removal.
  • Revoked: the resolver saw an RRSIG(DNSKEY) signed by this key over an RRSet containing it with REVOKE set to 1. The key MUST permanently be considered invalid as a trust anchor.
  • Removed: after a long hold-down the key's information may be purged. It MUST NOT be treated as a valid trust anchor.

Events drive the transitions: NewKey, AddTime, KeyRem, KeyPres, RevBit and RemTime.
sections.eli5: Each key goes through stages, like a new student: just arrived, waiting to be trusted, trusted, maybe lost for a bit, and finally retired and forgotten.

sections.title: Rollover Recipes and Trust Point Deletion
sections.content:
The suggested model is one active key, which signs the DNSKEY RRSet, and one stand-by key, which does not normally sign it. The stand-by private key can get extra protection, such as being locked in a safe or split among many parties.

  • Adding an anchor: generate a key pair, create a DNSKEY with the SEP and Zone Key bits set, add it to the RRSet, sign the RRSet only with the existing anchor A, and wait for resolvers to pick it up on the state table schedule.
  • Deleting an anchor: set the revocation bit on A and sign the RRSet with both A and B. Keep the revoked A in the RRSet for at least the remove hold-down time.
  • Rollover: with A active and B stand-by, add a new key C, set the revocation bit on A and sign the RRSet with A and B. Then A is revoked, B is active and C becomes stand-by when its hold-down expires. An active-key compromise is handled the same way.
  • Stand-by key compromise: add C, set the revocation bit on B, sign with A and B. B is revoked, A stays active and C becomes stand-by.

A trust point with all of its trust anchors revoked is considered deleted and treated as never configured. Without a superior configured trust point, data at and below it is insecure; with one, it is evaluated against that superior. A trust point subordinate to another MAY also be deleted by a resolver after 180 days, as a local decision. To do this cleanly, the operator gives the parent DS records for a new key and the old keys, then adds the new DNSKEY while revoking all old keys at once, and after 30 days stops publishing the revoked keys and asks for the old DS records to be removed.
sections.eli5: It is like always keeping a spare house key in a safe. If the main key is lost, you announce it is retired, bring out the spare, and have a new spare cut.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Key ownership and acceptance are separate. The zone owner creates and distributes keys, but whether a resolver accepts them is the resolver owner's decision. They MAY permit or prevent automatic updates for specific trust points, in which case they need a manual or other out-of-band way to update keys, which is outside this document.

The scheme permits recovery as long as at least one valid trust anchor stays uncompromised: with three keys, recovery is possible if two are compromised. If all trust anchor keys at a trust point are compromised, a manual or other out-of-band update of all resolvers is required.

Updating trust anchors from in-band information is potentially less secure than a manual process. Given the nature of DNS, the number of resolvers that would need an update after a compromise, and the lack of a standard management framework for DNS, the RFC judges it no worse than the existing situation. Rollover concerns not specific to this protocol are covered in RFC 4986.
sections.eli5: The owner of the computer still decides whether to follow the automatic key swaps. And if every single key is stolen, a person has to step in and fix it by hand.
